name: semantic-kernel

facts.description: Integrate cutting-edge LLM technology quickly and easily into your apps

title: Semantic Kernel: Microsoft's SDK for Building LLM-Powered AI Applications
answer: Semantic Kernel is Microsoft's open source SDK, written in C#, for integrating large language models into applications. It sits at the orchestration layer, connecting models from OpenAI, Google, Mistral, Amazon and others to your code through plugins, function calling and vector store connectors. The one thing to know before adopting it: it is a Microsoft project under the MIT licence with strong documentation, but several connectors, including Google, Mistral, Ollama and Bedrock, are still experimental and require suppressing preview warnings.

sections.body: Semantic Kernel is an open source framework from Microsoft, distributed under the MIT licence and hosted in the microsoft/semantic-kernel repository, which had accumulated 28,622 stars at the time of writing and showed a last push of 1 October 2026. Its stated purpose is to integrate cutting edge LLM technology quickly and easily into applications, and its primary language is C#. In the AI stack it occupies the orchestration layer rather than the model layer: it does not train or serve models itself, it sits between your application code and the chat completion services, plugins and vector stores that do the heavy lifting. The official documentation lives on Microsoft Learn, and the framework's core abstractions are the kernel, plugins, functions and connectors.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The framework's centre of gravity is chat completion, which the documentation describes as the most common AI service added to Semantic Kernel projects and as useful for chat bots and autonomous agents. Its strongest ground is function calling: Semantic Kernel serializes available functions and their parameters using JSON schema, sends them with the chat history, extracts function names and arguments from the model's response, invokes the matching code and returns results to the model, repeating until a chat message arrives or a maximum iteration count is reached. Plugins extend this to real work, either retrieving data for retrieval augmented generation or automating tasks, and existing APIs can be wrapped through native code, OpenAPI specifications or an MCP server. Vector store connectors handle data persistence, with built in mappers between data models and database schemas, though that area is marked as preview.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The learning curve depends heavily on what you already know. The documentation assumes working familiarity with C# or Python, since examples appear in both, and with the concept of dependency injection, which plugins are explicitly designed to work with. You do not need mathematics or model training knowledge, because the framework consumes hosted models rather than building them, but you do need to understand how chat completion APIs behave, what function calling is and how JSON schema describes parameters. The official site is generous to beginners in one respect: it walks through adding a chat completion service step by step, including running Ollama locally in Docker or loading an ONNX model, and it recommends starting with native code plugins before graduating to OpenAPI specifications as an application matures.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The connector ecosystem is broad. Official packages exist for Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, MistralAI, Google, HuggingFace, AzureAIInference, Ollama, Amazon and Onnx, and any provider that speaks the OpenAI chat completion API, such as LLM Studio, can be reached through the OpenAI connector. Anthropic models are available through Amazon Bedrock using the Amazon connector. Documentation on Microsoft Learn covers concepts, plugins, function calling behaviours, function invocation and vector store serialization, and the repository carries a substantial star count, which suggests an active audience. The caveat visible in the documentation itself is maturity: the Mistral, Google, Hugging Face, Azure AI Inference, Ollama and Bedrock connectors are all described as experimental and require suppressing the SKEXP0070 warning.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: Semantic Kernel leans toward rapid integration rather than low level performance control. Auto function calling is the default, so a developer can register plugins and let the framework describe functions to the model, invoke them and manage the back and forth without writing that loop. For production concerns, the framework exposes real levers: function choice behaviours let you allow, require or forbid model chosen functions, filters restrict which functions are advertised, concurrent invocation of parallel function calls can be enabled through FunctionChoiceBehaviorOptions, and direct serialization gives full control over how models map to a data store at some cost in portability. The documentation does not present benchmarks or latency figures, so claims about production performance beyond these configuration options are not settled by the official material.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The facts available show a Microsoft maintained project with a large star count and a documentation set hosted on Microsoft Learn, which indicates institutional backing and a reasonable expectation of continuity. The documentation notes that not all AI SDKs have an analogous concept to plugins, most offering only functions or tools, which positions Semantic Kernel as a more structured option for teams already inside the Microsoft ecosystem. What the facts and the site do not establish is how widely it is deployed in industry, which employers list it, or whether it is a current standard rather than a legacy choice. Anyone weighing it for a career should treat those questions as open and verify them against job listings rather than assume.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: Semantic Kernel is primarily a C# framework, with documentation and code samples also provided for Python, and it is designed to sit alongside whatever model provider a team already uses rather than replace it. The polyglot pattern it belongs to is the orchestration layer: your application logic stays in C# or Python, the model runs behind a connector, and plugins bridge the two, with OpenAPI specifications recommended as the way to share plugins across different programming languages and platforms once an application matures. It is not a training framework, a serving engine or a vector database, and the documentation positions it as the glue that lets an AI application plan and invoke APIs through the function calling features of modern language models.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: Several constraints are stated plainly. Function calling is supported only by a few AI connectors, and support among small language models remains limited. You cannot specify both excluded and included plugin or function lists at once, and an empty include list has no effect, so disabling function calling requires setting the behaviour to None, or NoneInvoke in Python to avoid clashing with the language keyword. OpenAPI plugins with duplicate parameter names are skipped with a warning, and version 3.1 specifications are downgraded to 3.0. Vector store serialization is marked preview. The official material does not state performance characteristics, deployment scale, long term support commitments or adoption numbers, and those questions remain unanswered by the sources consulted.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
